html:
Boiohaemum was the Latin name for Bohemia, in the heart of what is now the Czech Republic. It means "home of the Boii", the Celtic people who had lived there. The map shows it, spelled "Boihaenum", from 1 to 200 CE, when it was the seat of a Germanic kingdom.

Around 9 to 6 BCE the Germanic Marcomanni, under their king Maroboduus, moved into the area, which the Boii had left. Maroboduus had spent his youth in Rome and built a strong kingdom on the Roman model, with a large standing army. Rome planned to crush him in 6 CE, but the great revolt in Illyricum, the Bellum Batonianum, forced it to make peace. In 17 CE he fought Arminius, the victor of the Teutoburg Forest, and came off worse. Driven out in 19 CE, he lived out his life as an exile at Ravenna.

The Marcomanni and their neighbours the Quadi remained a power on the Danube frontier. Their invasion of the Roman Empire in the 160s set off the Marcomannic Wars with Marcus Aurelius. Slavs, the ancestors of the Czechs, settled the land in the 500s, but the old name lives on in "Bohemia".
